subject: english-literature
title: Giving Life and Going Large
welcome_lead: From talking trees to giant claims, master colourful devices.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on personification and hyperbole.
final_note: You can now spot personification and hyperbole at speed.

concepts.def: Phrase whose meaning is not literal.
Object that stands for an idea.
A joke using a word's double meaning.

walkthroughs.body_html: 'The wind whispered' gives the wind a human action. This is personification — it makes settings vivid.
'I've told you a million times' is hyperbole — clear exaggeration that's not meant literally.
'Deafening silence' is an oxymoron. 'Break a leg' is an idiom — meaning hidden inside the phrase.

mcqs.q: What did Romantic poets value in nature?
options: Romantic poets believed nature was full of fairies and elves.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
Romantic poets just liked to write about pretty landscapes.
Nature as a source of spiritual insight and emotional truth, accessed through imagination — not picturesque scenery for its own sake.
An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
Their account is undermined within the text by ignorance, bias, self-deception or deceit, so the reader must read against what they say.
An unreliable narrator is one who tells lies in the story.

mcqs.q: What is the dramatic function of a soliloquy?
options: A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
It reveals a character's inner thoughts directly to the audience while the character is alone on stage — a convention granting access to private psychology.
A soliloquy is any long speech a character gives.
An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
